title: Remember now your creator (Ecclesiastes 12:1–8)
hookLine: before the silver cord is loosed

lines: A HOUSE AT THE END OF THE DAY.
cards: A big old house, at the end of a day. The guards at the door tremble. The strong men are stooped.
The women who grind the grain have stopped, because too few are left. Those who look out of the windows find everything dim. The doors to the street are shut, and the sound of the mill is low.
Someone wakes at the first chirp of a bird. The almond tree is in bloom, all white. It sounds like a ghost story.
It's a riddle. He's describing a body growing old.

teach.h: REMEMBER, IN THE DAYS OF YOUTH.
teach.b: The poem opens, in the King James Bible: "Remember now thy Creator in the days of thy youth, while the evil days come not, nor the years draw nigh, when thou shalt say, I have no pleasure in them."

teach.h: A RIDDLE: HANDS, TEETH, EYES, HAIR.
teach.b: One old way of reading decodes the riddle of the house. The keepers of the house who tremble are the hands and arms. The strong men bowing are the legs and back.
The grinders that cease because they are few are the teeth. Those who look out of the windows are the eyes. Waking at the sound of a bird is light sleep in old age.
And the almond tree in white blossom is white hair. Not every reader takes each image the same way, and some hear a whole town falling into ruin as well as a body.

teach.h: THE SILVER CORD, THE GOLDEN BOWL.
teach.b: Then the images turn to endings: "Or ever the silver cord be loosed, or the golden bowl be broken." A lamp on a silver chain: the chain snaps, the golden bowl of oil shatters, the light goes out.
A pitcher breaks at the well. And then: "Then shall the dust return to the earth as it was: and the spirit shall return unto God who gave it."
Now back to the first word, remember. In Hebrew it's not only recalling a fact. It means keeping someone in mind and acting on it, the way God remembers Noah in the flood and sends the wind.

teach.h: THE SPIRIT SHALL RETURN UNTO GOD WHO GAVE IT.
teach.b: So remember your Creator isn't nostalgia. It's: live toward God now, while your hands are steady and your eyes are clear. The Preacher isn't trying to frighten the young.
He's urging them not to wait.

how: Ecclesiastes 12 is read at some Christian funerals, especially for older people, and its opening verse is often taught to young people in churches and youth groups as a call not to put faith off until later.

games.q: you're young. your hands are steady, your eyes are clear, and there's plenty of time for God later. what does the Preacher say?

remember your Creator now, in the days of your youth.
forget it: everything is breath anyway.
games.why: "remember now thy Creator in the days of thy youth, while the evil days come not." the Preacher's last poem is an urging not to wait.

practice: Feel your hands open and close slowly; notice your eyes taking in light, your ears catching small sounds. Whatever your age, your body can do things now that it may not always do.
If you pray, offer today's strength back to the One who gave it; if not, hold the thought that this strength is here now, and not forever.

wordCard.voice: Silver cord. The chain holding the lamp in the Preacher's riddle of old age, snapped just before the golden bowl breaks and the light goes out.

orig.note: Hebrew: remember. in the Bible, remembering usually leads to acting.
